title: Romantic music
wiki_lead:
Romantic music is a stylistic movement in Western Classical music associated with the period of the 19th century commonly referred to as the Romantic era (or Romantic period). It is closely related to the broader concept of Romanticism—the intellectual, artistic, and literary movement that became prominent in Western culture from about 1798 until 1837.
Romantic composers sought to create music that was individualistic, emotional, dramatic, and often programmatic; reflecting broader trends within the movements of Romantic literature, poetry, art, and philosophy. Romantic music was often ostensibly inspired by (or else sought to evoke) non-musical stimuli, such as nature, literature, poetry, super-natural elements, or the fine arts. It included features such as increased chromaticism and moved away from traditional forms.
grok_lead: Romantic music refers to the body of Western classical compositions produced roughly from 1800 to 1900, succeeding the Classical era and characterized by a heightened focus on emotional depth, personal expression, and individualism over structural restraint. Emerging as a reaction against the rationalism of the Enlightenment and the industrialization of society, it drew inspiration from literature, nature, and national folklore, fostering innovations like programmatic music that evoked extra-musical narratives and larger-scale orchestral works. Central to Romantic music were expanded forms such as expansive symphonies, virtuoso piano compositions, and operas that integrated leitmotifs and dramatic intensity, reflecting composers' pursuits of the sublime and the exotic. Key figures included Ludwig van Beethoven, who bridged Classical and Romantic styles through his symphonies; Franz Schubert, renowned for lieder blending poetry and melody; FrÃ©dÃ©ric Chopin, whose piano works captured nationalistic Polish elements; and Richard Wagner, whose music dramas revolutionized opera with continuous orchestration and mythological themes. Nationalism surged in the later period, evident in works by composers like Giuseppe Verdi in Italy and Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky in Russia, incorporating folk idioms amid political upheavals such as the revolutions of 1848. The era's defining achievements encompassed technical advancements like chromatic harmony and rubato, enabling greater expressive freedom, alongside the rise of the composer-performer virtuoso exemplified by Franz Liszt's transcriptions and concerts. By the late 19th century, transitions toward verismo opera and impressionism signaled the waning of pure Romanticism, yielding to modernist fragmentation around 1900.
